definition.text: The variety of living things found on farmland.

facts.text: Biodiversity on farms falls as varied landscapes are lost and native plants are replaced by crops.
The FAO estimates more than 40% of Earth's land surface is used for agriculture, making habitat loss the main driver of biodiversity loss.
Fallow land, grass margins and scrub strips between fields add habitat variety and so raise farm biodiversity.
Smaller fields have been linked to greater species richness.
In Asian rice, flowering strips beside fields cut insecticide spraying by 70% and raised yields by 5%, an economic advantage of 7.5%.
Low crop diversity can increase pests and pesticide resistance, causing ecological and economic losses.

definition.text: The variety of habitats and features across a farmed landscape, which supports a variety of species.

facts.text: Butterfly abundance has been found to increase with heterogeneity.
The Green Revolution, since 1966, spread a few crops such as wheat, rice and maize, reducing heterogeneity and local crop diversity.

definition.text: Growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons.

facts.text: It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance.
Growing the same crop year after year, monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialised pests.
Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to later crops.
Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon.
Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat.
Different crops spread the farmer's risk from bad weather.
In the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers.
US organic certification requires a crop rotation.

definition.text: A medieval European rotation dividing land into autumn crops, spring crops and a fallow field, rotated each year.

facts.text: Farmers in Europe moved to it from the two-field system between the 9th and 11th centuries, and it lasted until the 20th century.
Two thirds of the land was planted instead of half, and the legume crops improved people's nutrition.

definition.text: An 18th-century rotation of wheat, turnips, barley and clover that let livestock be kept all year.

facts.text: Charles Townshend popularised it, and it became a key development of the British Agricultural Revolution.

definition.text: The yield gain that rotated crops show compared with crops grown alone year after year.

facts.text: It arises mainly from relieving the problems of monoculture: better nutrition, less pest and weed stress and better soil structure.
